## 1. Goal

Extend the hand-worked golden cases to every policy and every named scenario, so each later policy issue has an independent oracle. Ahaana re-checks every case on paper.

## 2. Background

**From PRD §10 Golden cases:**

At least 10 small cases (3 to 6 jobs), each with the correct schedule worked out on paper and saved as `<case>.<policy>.expected.csv` next to its input `<case>.csv`: one per policy, plus big-job trap, priority starvation, memory hog, simultaneous finish and arrival, and a capacity-rejection case (not a schedule, see below). Ahaana redoes each schedule on paper, without looking at the program's output, and signs off in the PR before it merges.

**From BLUEPRINT §3.2 Four policies:**

Each policy is only a different heap key. The engine never changes.

| Policy | Key (best first) | Known weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FCFS | smallest arrival | Big job at the front blocks everyone |
| Static priority | largest priority | Low-priority jobs can starve |
| SJF | smallest duration | Long jobs can starve |
| Adaptive aging (ours) | largest 1000 × priority − alpha_milli × arrival (int64) | Big-memory jobs can still starve (fixed by 3.5) |

Every compare function finishes with the same tie-break: earlier arrival first, then lower id.

**From BLUEPRINT §3.3 (integer key):**

**Integer form (implemented).** α is stored as the integer `alpha_milli` = 1000·α (0 to 10,000). The heap key is the 64-bit integer

$$K_j = 1000\, b_j - \text{alpha\_milli} \cdot r_j$$

which is 1000 × (b_j − α·r_j), so it orders jobs exactly as the formula above, with no floating-point rounding and identical results on GCC, Clang and WebAssembly. |K_j| ≤ 9,000 + 10,000 × 10⁹ ≈ 10¹³, far inside int64. The live score is computed only when JSON is written: S_j(now) = b_j + alpha_milli·(now − r_j)/1000, from integers, printed with three decimals.

**From BLUEPRINT §3.5 Reservation:**

Based on EASY backfilling. At most one job holds a reservation at a time. Policy name: `reserve` (aging + reservation).

1. **Trigger.** The best job h does not fit, and it has waited at least T ticks (T is a user setting).
2. **Shadow time.** Walk the running jobs in order of finish time, adding back their resources, until h would fit. That finish time is h's guaranteed start, called the shadow time.
3. **Extra room.** Compute what CPU and memory will still be spare at the shadow time after h starts.
4. **Backfill rule.** Another job j may start now only if it fits now and either it finishes at or before the shadow time, or it fits inside the extra room (and then the extra room shrinks by j's demand).
5. **Start h** when the shadow time arrives. Then clear the reservation.

**From BLUEPRINT §5 Presets:**

| Preset | What it demonstrates |
| --- | --- |
| Big-job trap | Greedy's known worst case (Fan & Liang, Lemma 4.1); its own capacities so all small jobs fit together |
| Priority starvation | Static priority starving a low-priority job; aging rescuing it |
| Memory hog | Aging alone failing for a big-memory job; reservation fixing it |
| SJF starvation | A long job starved by a stream of short ones |
| Heavy load | Many jobs, high utilization, differences in average wait |
| Tiny case | 6 to 9 jobs, compared against the exact optimum |

## 3. Scope

**In scope:**

- ≥ 10 cases, 3–6 jobs: one per policy (fcfs, priority, sjf, aging, reserve; knapsack added in K-34), plus big-job trap, priority starvation, memory hog, simultaneous finish and arrival (10 schedule cases), plus the capacity-rejection console case
- Expected file per (case, policy) pair that the case is meant to show (e.g. memory hog for both aging and reserve)
- Worked timelines in `tests/cases/README.md`
- Ahaana's paper re-check of every case

**Out of scope:**

- Knapsack cases (K-34)
- Exact-solver cases (K-33)
- Making the cases pass (K-19, K-26)

## 4. Files

| Path | Create / modify | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/cases/*.csv` | create | Inputs |
| `tests/cases/*.<policy>.expected.csv` | create | Expected outputs |
| `tests/cases/README.md` | modify | Worked timelines |

## 5. Specification

Naming (D44): `<case>.csv` + `<case>.<policy>.expected.csv`; policy names `fcfs`, `priority`, `sjf`, `aging`, `reserve`. Defaults: alpha_milli 100, T 50, 16 cores, 32,768 MB unless the README states otherwise. Aging key: 1000·priority − alpha_milli·arrival, larger first. Capacity-rejection case (D54, decided in K-08): it is not a schedule. Files: `<case>.csv` (one job needs more than the machine has), `<case>.expected.exit` (`3`) and `<case>.expected.stderr` (the one-line text `CAPACITY_EXCEEDED: <message> (line N)`); no output file is written. Also add an API test (in `tests/c/test_engine.c` or a golden test) that the other jobs still schedule when the caller skips the bad one.

## 6. Step-by-step tasks

1. List the cases and which policies each one shows
2. Work each by hand in the README
3. Write the expected files
4. Ahaana redoes each case on paper
5. Fix any disagreement by re-deriving together

## 8. Acceptance criteria (Done when)

- [ ] ≥ 10 schedule cases, named `<case>.<policy>.expected.csv`, plus the capacity-rejection console case (`.expected.exit` = 3, `.expected.stderr`, no output file) and its API test
- [ ] Every policy and every named scenario covered
- [ ] Each has its worked timeline in the README
- [ ] Ahaana's paper check recorded for every case in the PR, **including the four FCFS cases from K-07 (tests/cases/fcfs_*), whose check was deferred here**

## 9. How to verify

```sh
ls tests/cases/*.expected.csv | wc -l
```
plus Ahaana's sign-off listing each case.

## 10. Viva notes

**Idea:** each case isolates one behaviour (e.g. the memory hog shows aging failing and reservation fixing it).
**Examiner question:** "Show me starvation." — The priority-starvation case under static priority vs aging.

## 11. Pitfalls

- Cases too big to work by hand
- Forgetting the tie-break when keys are equal
- Writing reserve cases before O-14 is decided (note the assumption)
